alt: Two addition polymer chains with an all-carbon backbone: poly(propene) has a methyl side group on every second backbone carbon, repeat unit -CH2-CH(CH3)-; poly(but-2-ene) has a methyl group on every backbone carbon, repeat unit -CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-, so the two are different polymers although both come from alkenes.
caption: Figure: repeat units of poly(propene) and poly(but-2-ene); the methyl groups are side groups, not part of the backbone

alt: Electrolysis cell for aluminium: carbon anodes dip into alumina dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 degrees C inside a carbon-lined steel cell that is the cathode; Al3+ ions are reduced to molten aluminium which collects at the bottom and is tapped off, while oxygen formed at the anodes burns the carbon to CO2, so the anodes are replaced.
caption: Figure: the aluminium extraction cell (alumina in molten cryolite, carbon electrodes)

alt: Boltzmann distribution at one temperature with two activation energies: the catalysed Ea line lies to the left of the uncatalysed Ea line, so the area of the curve beyond it, the molecules with enough energy to react, is larger, while the curve itself is unchanged.
caption: Figure: a catalyst lowers Ea, so more molecules have enough energy; the distribution itself is unchanged

alt: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures: both curves start at the origin and have the same area; the higher-temperature curve is lower and broader with its peak to the right, so the area beyond the activation energy Ea (the molecules able to react) is much larger.
caption: Figure: Boltzmann distributions at T₁ and a higher T₂; the area beyond Ea grows with temperature

alt: Born-Haber cycle for sodium chloride as an energy level diagram: from the elements at 0 the steps go up by +107 (atomisation of sodium), +494 (first ionisation energy of sodium) and +121 (atomisation of chlorine) to +722 kJ per mole, then down by 349 (electron affinity of chlorine) to the gaseous ions at +373, and finally down by 784 (lattice energy) to NaCl at −411, the same as the enthalpy of formation.
caption: Figure: Born-Haber cycle for NaCl (kJ per mole); the lattice energy is the step that completes the loop to ΔHf

alt: Bromoethane with hydroxide: in aqueous NaOH, OH minus uses a lone pair to attack the delta-plus carbon while the C-Br bond breaks, giving ethanol and Br minus (substitution); in ethanolic NaOH, OH minus removes an H from the neighbouring carbon, the C-H electrons form C=C and Br minus leaves, giving ethene, water and Br minus (elimination).
caption: Figure: substitution and elimination of bromoethane with hydroxide, drawn with curly arrows

alt: Temperature against time for zinc displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate: the solution is steady at 21 °C, zinc is added at 4 min, the temperature rises quickly then cools slowly; extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing gives 40.6 °C, so the corrected temperature change is 19.6 °C.
caption: Figure: extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing gives the corrected ΔT (19.6 °C)

alt: Cis and trans but-2-ene: in the cis isomer the two CH3 groups are on the same side of the C=C double bond (and the two H atoms on the other side); in the trans isomer the CH3 groups are on opposite sides. There is no rotation about the double bond, so they are different molecules.
caption: Figure: cis and trans isomers of but-2-ene; the double bond cannot rotate

alt: Combustion calorimetry: a spirit burner containing ethanol heats 150.0 g of water in a copper can under a clamp, with a thermometer in the water; the water rises by 24.0 degrees C while 0.92 g (0.0200 mol) of ethanol burns, and heat lost to the air makes the measured enthalpy change too small.
caption: Figure: simple combustion calorimeter (spirit burner and copper can) as in Example 2

alt: Shapes of four complex ions: [Ag(NH3)2]+ is linear with 180 degrees between the two ligands; [CuCl4]2- is tetrahedral at 109.5 degrees; cisplatin [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] is square planar with 90 degrees, the two NH3 next to each other; [Cu(H2O)6]2+ is octahedral with 90 degrees between neighbouring water ligands.
caption: Figure: linear, tetrahedral, square planar and octahedral complexes

alt: Copper refining cell: a thick impure copper anode and a thin pure copper cathode in acidified copper(II) sulfate; copper dissolves from the anode as Cu2+ and is deposited as pure copper on the cathode, so the anode loses mass and the cathode gains mass, while unreactive silver, gold and platinum fall below the anode as anode sludge.
caption: Figure: electrolytic refining of copper

alt: Energy diagram of d orbitals: in a free transition metal ion the five d orbitals have the same energy; in an octahedral complex the ligands split them into three lower and two higher orbitals with an energy gap ΔE. A photon of visible light with energy ΔE is absorbed when an electron moves up, so the complex appears coloured with the remaining wavelengths.
caption: Figure: d-orbital splitting in a complex; absorption of light across the gap ΔE gives colour

alt: Two graphs for a reversible reaction starting from reactants only: on the left the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they meet and stay equal (dynamic equilibrium); on the right the reactant concentration falls and the product concentration rises until both become constant, at different values.
caption: Figure: at equilibrium the rates are equal and the concentrations stay constant (they need not be equal)

alt: Electrophilic addition of HBr to propene in two steps: the C=C pi electrons attack the H of H-Br, which breaks to give Br minus, leaving a secondary carbocation CH3-CH+-CH3; the bromide ion then donates a lone pair to the positive carbon, giving 2-bromopropane as the major product.
caption: Figure: electrophilic addition of HBr to propene, with curly arrows and the secondary carbocation intermediate

alt: The two enantiomers of lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH: each has a central chiral carbon bonded to COOH, CH3, OH and H; the two molecules are mirror images across a dashed mirror plane, with OH on a wedge and H on a hashed bond, and cannot be superimposed.
caption: Figure: a chiral carbon with four different groups gives two non-superimposable mirror images

alt: Energy profile of an exothermic reaction: reactants at a higher energy than products; the catalysed path has a lower peak, so a smaller activation energy, but starts and ends at the same energy levels, so the enthalpy change is unchanged.
caption: Figure: a catalyst lowers the activation energy; reactant and product levels, and ΔH, are the same

alt: Energy profile for homogeneous catalysis: the uncatalysed route has one high peak; the catalysed route has two lower peaks with a dip between them for an intermediate, the catalyst reacting in step 1 and being regenerated in step 2, and both end at the same product energy.
caption: Figure: homogeneous catalysis gives a two-step route with two lower activation energies

alt: Ethene bonding: the two carbon atoms are joined by a sigma bond from end-on overlap along the C-C axis, plus a pi bond from sideways overlap of two p orbitals with one lobe above and one below the plane of the molecule; with four C-H sigma bonds, C2H4 has 5 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond.
caption: Figure: the sigma and pi bonds of the C=C double bond in ethene

alt: Concentration-time curve for a first-order reaction with half-life 345 s starting at 0.0800 mol per dm³: the concentration is 0.0400 at 345 s, 0.0200 at 690 s and 0.0100 at 1035 s, so every half-life is the same length, which proves first order.
caption: Figure: a first-order reaction has a constant half-life (345 s here)

alt: Fractional distillation column: heated crude oil vapour enters near the bottom; the column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top, so the fractions leave at different heights, from the top refinery gases (C1-C4), gasoline (C5-C10), naphtha (C7-C10), kerosene (C10-C16), diesel (C14-C20) to the residue above C20 at the bottom; boiling point and molecule size rise down the column.
caption: Figure: fractional distillation of crude oil, with the carbon range and typical use of each fraction

alt: Free-radical substitution of methane by chlorine: UV light splits Cl2 into two chlorine radicals (initiation); in propagation Cl radical plus CH4 gives HCl and a methyl radical, and the methyl radical plus Cl2 gives CH3Cl and a new Cl radical, so the chain repeats; termination steps, Cl with Cl, CH3 with Cl or CH3 with CH3, remove two radicals and leave none.
caption: Figure: the radical chain mechanism for CH₄ + Cl₂, showing the propagation cycle

alt: Layout of a gas chromatograph: carrier gas sweeps the vaporised sample from the heated injection port into a column in an oven, where components partition between the gas and a liquid stationary phase; each leaves at its own retention time and is sensed by the detector, which sends a signal to the recorder that draws the chromatogram.
caption: Figure: how a gas-liquid chromatograph is arranged, from injection to chromatogram

alt: Gas chromatogram of three alcohols as triangular peaks: ethanol (base 0.6 min, height 52 mm, area 15.6, 56.5 percent), propan-1-ol (0.8 min, 18 mm, 7.2, 26.1 percent) and butan-1-ol (1.0 min, 9.6 mm, 4.8, 17.4 percent); percentages come from peak areas, not heights.
caption: Figure: composition from peak areas (half base times height) for the mixture in Example 2

alt: Gibbs energy change against temperature for two reactions: CaCO3 decomposition (ΔH +178, ΔS +0.1604 kJ per K per mol) falls with temperature, from +130 kJ per mol at 298 K to zero at 1110 K; ammonia synthesis (ΔH −92.2, ΔS −0.1988) rises, from −33.0 kJ per mol at 298 K to zero at 464 K. The gradient is minus ΔS and the intercept is ΔH.
caption: Figure: ΔG against T is a straight line with gradient −ΔS and intercept ΔH; it crosses zero at T = ΔH/ΔS

alt: Titration curve of 20.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol per dm3 glycine hydrochloride with NaOH: the pH starts near 1.7, has a first buffer region around pH 2.34, rises steeply at the first equivalence point (20.0 cm3, pH 5.97, the isoelectric point), has a second buffer region around pH 9.60, and rises again to about pH 11 at the second equivalence point (40.0 cm3).
caption: Figure: glycine titration curve with two buffer regions and two equivalence points (pKa 2.34 and 9.60)

alt: Enthalpy of solution from the lesson examples: MgSO4 -150 kJ per mol (exothermic, soluble) but BaSO4 +10 (endothermic, insoluble), so sulfates get less soluble down Group 2; Mg(OH)2 +155 but Ba(OH)2 +40, less endothermic, so hydroxides get more soluble down the group.
caption: Figure: ΔH sol for Mg and Ba sulfates and hydroxides (values from Examples 2 and 3)

alt: Flow diagram of the Haber process: nitrogen and hydrogen are compressed to about 200 atm, passed over an iron catalyst at 400-450 degrees C in the converter, then cooled so ammonia liquefies and is removed; the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back to the compressor.
caption: Figure: the Haber process as a flow of conditions, with recycling of unreacted gases

alt: Bar chart of halogen bond energies in kJ per mol: F-F 158, Cl-Cl 242, Br-Br 193, I-I 151; the energy falls from chlorine to iodine as atoms get larger, but fluorine is out of order because repulsion between lone pairs on its small atoms weakens the bond.
caption: Figure: halogen X–X bond energies; F–F is anomalously weak

alt: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to ethanal: the carbon lone pair of CN minus attacks the delta-plus carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi bond moves onto oxygen, giving an alkoxide intermediate CH3CH(O minus)CN; the O minus then takes the H of H-CN, giving 2-hydroxypropanenitrile and regenerating CN minus.
caption: Figure: nucleophilic addition of HCN to ethanal, in two steps, with cyanide as the catalyst

alt: Hess cycle for the formation of propane from combustion data: carbon and hydrogen burn directly to 3CO2 and 4H2O with a total of −2326 kJ (3 × −394 plus 4 × −286), while propane burns to the same products with −2219 kJ, so the enthalpy of formation of propane is −2326 − (−2219) = −107 kJ per mole.
caption: Figure: energy cycle using combustion data; the enthalpy of formation is the difference between the two routes

alt: Boiling points in degrees Celsius of the hydrides of Groups 14 to 17 for periods 2 to 4: Group 14 rises steadily CH4 −162, SiH4 −112, GeH4 −88; but in Groups 15, 16 and 17 the period-2 hydrides NH3 (−33), H2O (100) and HF (20) are far higher than the next member, because of hydrogen bonding.
caption: Figure: boiling points of hydrides; NH₃, H₂O and HF stand out because they form hydrogen bonds

alt: Hydrogen bonding in water: the central water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds, two from its partially positive hydrogen atoms to the oxygen of molecules below, and two from the hydrogen atoms of molecules above to the lone pairs on its own oxygen.
caption: Figure: hydrogen bonds (dashed) between water molecules; each molecule can form up to four

alt: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte: hydrogen is oxidised at the negative porous platinum-catalysed anode (H2 to 2H+ + 2e-), H+ ions pass through the electrolyte to the positive cathode where oxygen is reduced to water (O2 + 4H+ + 4e- to 2H2O), and electrons travel through the external circuit; the cell potential is 1.23 V.
caption: Figure: hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell with an acid electrolyte (E°cell = 1.23 V)

alt: First ionisation energy across Period 3 in kJ per mole: Na 494, Mg 736, Al 577, Si 786, P 1060, S 1000, Cl 1260, Ar 1520. The general rise is interrupted by a dip from Mg to Al (the 3p electron is higher in energy than 3s) and a dip from P to S (the first paired 3p electron is repelled).
caption: Figure: first ionisation energies across Period 3, with the two dips explained

alt: Graph of log10 of the successive ionisation energies of sodium against the number of electrons removed: one electron is removed easily (494 kJ per mole), then eight electrons with slowly rising values from 4560 to 28 900, then a huge jump to 141 000 and 159 000 for the last two, showing the 2,8,1 shell structure.
caption: Figure: successive ionisation energies of sodium; each step up marks a new shell closer to the nucleus

alt: Chart of characteristic infrared absorption ranges in cm-1: O-H alcohol 3200-3600, O-H acid 2500-3000, N-H 3300-3500, C-H 2850-2950, C≡N 2200-2250, C=O ester 1710-1750, carbonyl 1670-1740, amide 1640-1690, C=C 1500-1680 and C-O 1040-1300; the fingerprint region lies below 1500.
caption: Figure: characteristic IR absorption ranges from the data table; the C=O ranges overlap, so position is only a hint

alt: Infrared spectrum of the unknown C4H8O2 from the worked example: a medium C-H trough at 2950 cm-1, a strong sharp C=O trough at 1740 (ester range 1710-1750) and a strong C-O trough at 1240, with no broad O-H absorption between 2500 and 3600, so the compound is an ester, not an acid or alcohol.
caption: Figure: IR spectrum of the ester in Example 1 (peaks at 2950, 1740 and 1240 cm⁻¹; no O–H)

alt: Four lattice types: a giant ionic layer with alternating Na+ and Cl- ions; a giant metallic lattice of positive ions with delocalised electrons between them; graphite as stacked layers with strong covalent bonds inside each layer and weak forces between layers; and diamond with each carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others.
caption: Figure: ionic, metallic, graphite and diamond lattices (schematic)

alt: Mass spectrum of boron: a short peak at m/e 10 with relative abundance 19.9 and a tall peak at m/e 11 with relative abundance 80.1, giving a relative atomic mass of about 10.8.
caption: Figure: mass spectrum of boron; each peak is one isotope and its height is its abundance

alt: Mass spectrum of butanone (Mr 72): peaks at m/e 29 (abundance 15, C2H5+), 43 (100, the base peak, CH3CO+), 57 (8, C2H5CO+) and 72 (20, the molecular ion), so the highest m/e is the relative molecular mass and the tallest peak is not the molecular ion.
caption: Figure: mass spectrum of butanone; the molecular ion is at m/e 72 and the base peak at 43

alt: Mass spectrum pattern of chloroethane: molecular ion peaks at m/e 64 (C2H5 with chlorine-35) and 66 (chlorine-37) in the height ratio 3 to 1, the signature of one chlorine atom.
caption: Figure: one chlorine atom gives M and M+2 peaks in the ratio 3 : 1

alt: Membrane cell for brine: concentrated sodium chloride enters the anode compartment where chloride ions form chlorine (2Cl- to Cl2 + 2e-); water enters the cathode compartment where hydrogen and hydroxide ions form; sodium ions pass through the ion-exchange membrane to the cathode side to give sodium hydroxide solution, and the membrane keeps chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide apart.
caption: Figure: membrane cell producing chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide from brine

alt: Nitration of benzene in two steps: a curly arrow from the delocalised ring to the N of NO2 plus gives an intermediate with H and NO2 on one carbon and the positive charge delocalised over the other five; a curly arrow from the C-H bond restores the ring, releasing H plus (which regenerates H2SO4) and giving nitrobenzene.
caption: Figure: electrophilic substitution of benzene by NO₂⁺, showing the intermediate and the restored ring

alt: Nylon-6,6: hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid join by condensation, losing water at each amide link CO-NH; in the solid, the delta-plus hydrogen of an N-H group on one chain forms a hydrogen bond (dashed) with the delta-minus oxygen of a C=O group on the neighbouring chain, which makes the polyamide strong with a high melting point.
caption: Figure: nylon-6,6 amide links and the hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains

alt: Sub-shell energy ladder for iron (26 electrons) drawn as orbital boxes with spin arrows: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s and 3p are full, 4s is full and sits slightly below 3d, and the five 3d boxes hold six electrons, one paired and four unpaired, giving 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6 4s2.
caption: Figure: electron configuration of iron in boxes; 4s is below 3d, and singly occupied boxes fill before pairing

alt: Atomic and ionic radii across Period 3: atomic radius falls steadily from 0.186 nm for Na to 0.099 nm for Cl; the cations Na+ to Si4+ are much smaller (0.095 down to 0.041 nm) while the anions P3-, S2- and Cl- are larger than their atoms (0.212, 0.184, 0.181 nm), so ionic radius jumps up between Si4+ and P3-.
caption: Figure: atomic and ionic radii across Period 3 (data from the table above)

alt: Bar chart of melting points across Period 3 in kelvin: Na 371, Mg 922, Al 933 (giant metallic, rising), Si 1687 (giant covalent, highest), then P4 317, S8 388, Cl2 172 and Ar 84 (simple molecules or atoms, low).
caption: Figure: melting points across Period 3; metals rise to Al, Si (giant covalent) is highest, molecular elements are low

alt: Schematic proton NMR spectrum of ethanol: a triplet for CH3 near 1.2 ppm with area 3, a singlet for OH near 2.6 ppm with area 1, and a quartet for CH2 near 3.7 ppm with area 2; the n + 1 rule gives the splitting, and TMS is the reference at 0 ppm.
caption: Figure: schematic proton NMR spectrum of ethanol (areas 3 : 2 : 1)

alt: Reaction profile with an intermediate for the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone: step 1, involving propanone and H+, has the higher activation energy and is the slow rate-determining step; step 2, involving iodine, has a lower peak and is fast, which is why the rate equation is rate = k[propanone][H+] and the reaction is zero order in iodine.
caption: Figure: a two-step profile; the slow step with the higher peak sets the rate equation

alt: Volume of carbon dioxide against time for 0.300 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid: the curve rises steeply then levels at 72 cm³, and a dashed tangent at t = 0 through (30 s, 54 cm³) has gradient 1.8 cm³ per second, the initial rate.
caption: Figure: gas volume against time; the tangent at t = 0 gives the initial rate (1.8 cm³ s⁻¹)

alt: Two graph panels for orders 0, 1 and 2. Concentration against time: zero order is a straight falling line, first order a curve with constant half-life, second order a curve that flattens more slowly. Rate against concentration: zero order is horizontal, first order a straight line through the origin, second order curves upward.
caption: Figure: concentration-time and rate-concentration graphs for zero, first and second order

alt: Two set-ups for oxidising ethanol with acidified dichromate: under reflux, a vertical water-cooled condenser sits on the flask so vapour condenses and runs back, giving the carboxylic acid; for distillation, the flask is fitted with a thermometer and a sloping condenser leading to a receiver, so the lower-boiling aldehyde ethanal (bp 21 degrees C) is collected before it is oxidised further.
caption: Figure: heating under reflux (acid) compared with distilling off the product (aldehyde)

alt: Measuring the standard electrode potential of copper: on the left the standard hydrogen electrode (platinum in 1.00 mol per dm³ H+ with hydrogen gas at 101 kPa bubbling over it) is connected through a high-resistance voltmeter and a salt bridge to a copper electrode in 1.00 mol per dm³ Cu2+; the voltmeter reads +0.34 V, the E standard of Cu2+/Cu.
caption: Figure: the standard hydrogen electrode (left) joined to a Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell; the reading is E⦵(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V

alt: Two reaction profiles for halogenoalkane hydrolysis: SN2 has a single peak at the transition state, with the reactants RX and hydroxide passing directly to products; SN1 has two peaks with a dip between them for the carbocation intermediate, and the first step, forming the carbocation, has the higher peak so it is the slow step.
caption: Figure: SN2 has a transition state; SN1 has a real intermediate and a slow first step

alt: Enthalpy cycles for dissolving: for NaCl the lattice must be broken (+787 kJ per mol) and the ions hydrated (-406 + -364 = -770), so the enthalpy of solution is +17, slightly endothermic; for MgCl2 breaking the lattice costs +2526 and hydration gives -1921 + 2(-364) = -2649, so the enthalpy of solution is -123, exothermic.
caption: Figure: enthalpy of solution as lattice breaking plus hydration, for NaCl (+17) and MgCl₂ (−123 kJ mol⁻¹)

alt: Steam distillation apparatus: a flask of boiling water with a safety tube makes steam, which is passed through a tube to the bottom of a second flask holding plant material and water; the mixed vapour of oil and water goes through a water-cooled condenser into a receiver as a cloudy distillate that forms two layers, and the oil is separated with a separating funnel.
caption: Figure: steam distillation of an essential oil, from steam generator to distillate

alt: Titration apparatus: a burette on a stand holds 0.100 mol per dm3 sulfuric acid above a conical flask containing 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide from a pipette plus indicator, standing on a white tile; acid is added while swirling until the colour changes, and the titre is the final minus the initial burette reading (mean of concordant titres 22.42 cm3).
caption: Figure: titration set-up for Example 1 (acid in the burette, 25.0 cm³ of alkali in the flask)

alt: pH against volume of base for 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol per dm³ acid and 0.100 mol per dm³ base: hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide starts at pH 1 and has equivalence at pH 7; ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide starts near pH 3 and has equivalence at pH 8.73; hydrochloric acid with ammonia has equivalence at pH 5.28. All three have equivalence at 25.0 cm³.
caption: Figure: three titration curves; the equivalence point is at 25.0 cm³ for each but at different pH values

alt: Titration curve of 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol per dm³ ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide: the half-equivalence point at 12.5 cm³ has pH 4.76, equal to the pKa; the phenolphthalein range 8.3 to 10.0 lies on the steep section near 25.0 cm³, while the methyl orange range 2.9 to 4.6 lies in the buffer region, so only phenolphthalein gives a sharp end-point.
caption: Figure: weak acid with strong base: pH = pKa at half-equivalence; the shaded bands are two indicator ranges

alt: TLC plate with solvent front 7.5 cm above the baseline: reference dyes P, Q and R have spots at 1.8, 4.2 and 6.0 cm (Rf 0.24, 0.56 and 0.80) and the mixture S has two spots at 1.8 cm and 6.0 cm, matching P and R, so S contains P and R but not Q.
caption: Figure: TLC plate for the food-colouring example; spots are compared by Rf on the same plate

alt: Six molecule shapes with bond angles: CO2 linear 180 degrees; BF3 trigonal planar 120 degrees; CH4 tetrahedral 109.5 degrees; NH3 pyramidal 107 degrees with one lone pair on top; H2O bent 104.5 degrees with two lone pairs; SF6 octahedral 90 degrees. Wedges come towards the viewer and hashed lines go away.
caption: Figure: shapes and bond angles from VSEPR; lone pairs are pairs of dots, which squeeze the bond angle

alt: Zinc-copper cell with a high-resistance voltmeter reading 1.10 V: a zinc electrode in 1.00 mol per dm³ zinc ions is the negative electrode where zinc is oxidised, a copper electrode in 1.00 mol per dm³ copper ions is the positive electrode where copper ions are reduced, a salt bridge joins the beakers and electrons flow through the wire from zinc to copper.
caption: Figure: the zinc-copper cell; electrons flow from the negative zinc electrode to the positive copper electrode
